The Room and the Rest

Burst Monitor · the weekly read, from the Friday, September 25 close

The Room and the Rest

The S&P 500 gained 1.2% this week and finished 0.7% below its record. The typical stock lost 0.7%. A room of about seventy stocks built around the AI hardware supply chain, with Apple at its center, supplied half of the gain. Three large stocks outside it, Meta, Microsoft and AMD, supplied the other half. The other 430 stocks, taken together, subtracted from it. Underneath, the instrument's parts pulled further apart all week, and none of the decisive markers of a break fired.

Where we left off · three reads this week, none shared until now

Sunday, Sep 20
The Rebound Came Back Alone. The field was floating with no shared crest, and the week ended at a fork: a release (a closure fires and the field refills) or a roll-through (the rhythm turns back down with no closure).
Wednesday, Sep 23
The Quiet Slide, from Monday's close. It sharpened the fork into catch-up (the typical stock climbs to meet the index) or catch-down (the index takes the slide its stocks already took). It leaned slightly toward catch-up and named the markers that would tell the roads apart. This edition keeps that read's teaching and grades its markers.
Friday, Sep 25
A notebook entry from Wednesday's close. It found the AI-hardware room: seventy stocks that had assembled over about 45 sessions and crested together on Tuesday. The lean moved to "even, tilting catch-down," and a ten-session test on that room was registered before the instrument had seen the result.
The feed
Our price provider served no Tuesday, Sep 22 close for most stocks for three days. The collector that writes the daily record refused the broken day, but that Thursday morning's board ran on a fake flat Tuesday, and its output has been superseded. The bar was repaired on Friday from official exchange closes and checked against the names the provider did have. Everything here uses the repaired Tuesday.

Chapter 1 · Friday, Sep 18 → Friday, Sep 25

One good day

The week's gain came on Monday. Meta rose 11% on the launch of its Muse AI agent and chipmakers followed, lifting the S&P 500 1.49%. On Tuesday the same agent sank the stocks it threatens: banks, brokers, insurers and travel companies. JPMorgan fell 3.4% and Schwab more than 5%. The index was flat.

Wednesday brought the strongest business-activity survey in over five years, which revived fears of another rate hike. The five-year Treasury yield touched 5% for the first time since 2007 and the index fell 0.75%. A cargo ship was struck in the Strait of Hormuz that day. On Thursday oil rose, the ten-year yield reached about 5.19%, its highest since 2007, and President Trump and Xi Jinping extended their trade truce through January. The index finished flat. On Friday oil fell 2%, consumer sentiment dropped to a four-month low, and the index rose 0.51% to 7,743.41.

Add the days up and the index gained 1.22%. The typical stock lost 0.70%. Weighting every stock equally gives −0.25%, and weighting by market value, as the index does, gives +1.26%. Only 43% of stocks rose. After Monday the index slipped 0.26% and the median stock fell 0.88%. The ten largest companies, 40% of the index's value, supplied 60% of the week's value-weighted gain of 1.26 points.

By sector the week split in two. Technology's median stock rose 1.8%, and the sector supplied 1.17 of the 1.26 points of value-weighted gain. Industrials and healthcare also gained. Financials fell 2.2% on the week, most of it from Tuesday on, and only 17% of them rose. Utilities fell 3.4% as yields climbed, and 29 of the 31 finished lower. Energy fell 3.3% with oil: it lost ground on the days oil fell and gained on the two days yields jumped. Communication services shows both sides. Its median stock lost 1.6%, but Meta's 13% gain made it the second-largest contributor to the index.

Since the record

The index closed at its record on August 13. Six weeks later it is 0.7% below it. The equal-weight average is 4.7% below, the typical stock is 6.1% below, and 77% of the 503 companies are lower than they were that day.

Wednesday's read measured how unusual this gap is. It took every session since 2000 when the S&P 500 sat within 1.5% of its 52-week closing high, with that high set between one week and three months earlier. There are now 818 such sessions, this week's five included. In each one it compared the median stock's move since the high with the index's. Normally the two sit within about a point of each other. On Monday the gap was −5.0 points, the widest on the record. By Friday it was −5.4. Every session this week sits past the old extreme of −2.8 points, set on December 24, 2024.

Chapter 2 · August 25 → September 25

Twenty-two days without a crest

Every stock has a short rhythm. It rises for a week or two, tops out, falls back and turns up again. The Burst Monitor tracks that rhythm for each company. On most days enough of them reach the top of their rhythm on the same day that the instrument logs a closure. The rule is at least 8% of the stocks in its pool, which counts about 750 names including recent members, so 59 names today.

Closures are the market's ordinary heartbeat: 4,207 of them in 6,723 sessions since 2000, usually a day apart. A stretch with none is a silence. The last closure was August 25, when 71 stocks topped out together. The 22 sessions since have been silent.

A closure day · many names peak together

When enough stocks (8% or more) reach the top of their own short swing on the same day, the instrument logs a closure. The names involved get a jolt of participation pressure, and on the map they sink back below the floor.

A silence · no shared peak

When the swings stop lining up, nothing refills the pressure. Each name's participation fades on a fixed half-life of 21 sessions, and the whole field drifts up off the floor together. The instrument calls that drift the float.

A silence ends when the count of stocks cresting together reaches the bar. The instrument keeps that count for every day, so we can see how close the market came. This week it never came close. Tuesday was the nearest, with 48 names against a bar of 59. Friday's build had Tuesday at 55; the newest few days of this ledger are revised as sessions arrive. The closest miss of the whole silence is still September 3, at 55.

Twenty-two sessions is long. Since 2000, 19 silences have lasted this long. In all 19 the S&P 500 was lower by the 22nd session, by a median 10.4%. The closest case was October 2016, when the index was flat. In this one the index is up 0.9% since August 25 and the median stock is down 5.4%. The typical stock has done what it usually does in a silence, a little more mildly. The index has not.

Across 98 silences of eight sessions or more, the index was up at that point in a handful of cases, and in none of them had the typical stock fallen more than 2%. September 3 is now four names short of the bar (55 against 59), further than on Wednesday, so this edition counts the silence from August 25.

Silences are usually slides. This one is a slide the index still hasn't joined.

How silences end

A silence ends with a closure, the day the rhythms line up again. The instrument calls that the release. Of the 19 silences that reached 22 sessions, 15 ended on a day the S&P 500 rose. The 19 that reached 22 sessions lasted a median of 27, and three in four were over by 32. The longest ran 47. Inside silences of 15 sessions or more, a closure followed within ten sessions 73% of the time and within fifteen 88% of the time.

The catch from Wednesday still holds. Every one of those releases came after the index had fallen, so they tended to end near a low. Measured from the 22nd session, the next month's median was +3.8% (74% up), with a 10th percentile of −5.6%, a little wider than an ordinary session's −4.7%. This silence has no index drop to recover from. Nothing in the record starts where the index is now.

Chapter 3 · a group of stocks followed through the week

Seventy stocks carried the index

A second instrument, Burst Currents, sorts the 503 names each day into rooms: groups of stocks that have been moving with each other rather than with the market as a whole. Rooms are not sectors. They are built from how stocks actually traded over the past quarter, and they reshuffle a good deal from day to day.

On Friday's build, reading Wednesday's close, one room stood out. It held 70 stocks and about a fifth of the index's value, and Apple alone was 35% of it. It is not a pure technology group (29 of the 70 are technology companies, and Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom sit elsewhere), but its core is the AI hardware supply chain: memory and storage (Micron, Seagate, Western Digital, Sandisk), chip equipment (Lam, Applied Materials, KLA), optical and networking parts (Coherent, Lumentum, Ciena), contract manufacturers (Flex, Jabil) and the industrial firms building data-center power (Caterpillar, GE Vernova, Eaton, Vertiv). Traced backward, it assembled over about six weeks. The supply-chain seed came together in early August, Apple and other large technology names joined in late August, and a group of financial and service companies joined in September. We froze those 70 names on Wednesday and followed them through Friday.

The room did half of the index's work this week. Weighted by market value it gained 3.2%, and it supplied half of the gain while holding a fifth of the value. The other half came from three large stocks outside it: Meta (0.35 points), Microsoft (0.24) and AMD (0.18). The remaining 430 stocks together subtracted 0.13 points. The room also held together. On Thursday and Friday 65 of the 70 frozen names were still in one room. By Friday five had drifted out (Best Buy, Kroger, Synopsys, Steel Dynamics, Williams) and six had joined (Linde, Eli Lilly, Monolithic Power, Philip Morris, UPS, Yum). Rooms usually reshuffle more than that in two sessions; a study on Monday's river found adjacent days' rooms agree only about 0.58 on the usual measure. These two days came after the freeze, so the room could not look tight simply because we picked it on its best day.

A crest traveling through the room

The clock from Wednesday's read shows why the room matters for the fork. Each stock's price is compared with its own 20-session average, and its place in that swing becomes a position between the trough (the bottom of the swing) and home (the top). The chart below follows three parts of the room and the rest of the market through the two weeks since the Fed decision.

The crest is moving through the supply chain in order: the heavy core first, then the equipment makers, then the industrials. Measured by market value, the room is coherent (a hand strength of 0.73 on the scale Chapter 5 explains) and sits just past home, 0.12 of a cycle beyond the crest. Counted name by name it is not coherent (0.23), because its financial and service members are scattered around the dial. That is the leaders-and-crowd split from Wednesday's read, happening inside one room.

Friday's notebook registered a test on this room before the instrument had seen the next session: follow it for ten sessions, from September 24 to October 7. Two sessions are in.

The test calls the room pulled if (a) and (b) both hold at session ten. That would mean the room held together while its heavy core rolled into its descent, the catch-down mechanism in miniature. It calls the room peeled if the financial and service half leaves while the technology core stays. Anything else is mixed. For now the room is intact, and its core is past the crest but not yet falling.

The rest of Currents: nine rooms on Friday (7.9 effective), about where Monday stood. Day-to-day room identity fell from 0.79 on Tuesday to 0.58 on Friday, so the rooms reshuffled more as the week went on. How often technology names are led from inside their own rooms rather than by the market rose to 80%, the 99th percentile of the river's window, from 67% on Wednesday's tile. Technology is running its own show, near the top of the window's range.

Chapter 4 · the motion map, July 27 → September 25

The field floats, and the six-month crowd lets go

The motion map is the instrument's main picture. It places all 503 companies on one chart every day and plays the days as a film. What matters is how the dots move, more than where any one of them sits.

Up and down

Height is how much a company is taking part in the market's shared moves, compared with its own normal. The white floor is normal. Above it the company is quieter than usual, below it busier and more pressed. A closure pushes names down through the floor. In a silence they drift back up.

Left and right

Width is how closely a company's participation tracks the market's own pulse. Right means tightly tied, moving with the crowd. Left means loosely tied. The upper-left corner, quiet and on its own, is the breakaway. The upper-right corner, quiet but still tied, is the strain. Between them, out of range but only partly tied, is an unnamed middle strip.

Two memories

"Normal" needs a memory. The instrument reads every stock twice: against the past year (252 sessions) and against the past six months (126). The same day can look different through each.

The room, on the map

The player below can outline the 70 stocks from Chapter 3. On the map they are spread out like everyone else. A room shows up on the clock (Chapter 5) far more than on the map.

The one-year memory: the float nearly complete

Through the one-year memory the float went on as it had for three weeks. The share of names quieter than their norm rose from 90% to 96%. Names below the floor fell from 50 to 20, and none dived through it, because dives happen only on closure days. The breakaway corner grew from 128 to 209, with 81 names in and none out over five sessions. The 81 newcomers came from all eleven sectors and hold a quarter of the index's value. The largest were Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Exxon, Bank of America and Thermo Fisher. The strain corner is empty. Mean coupling to the market's pulse slipped from −0.05 to −0.06, still falling rather than rising.

The compass, which measures how uniformly the whole field moved over five sessions, reads 0.96 on a 0-to-1 scale, heading almost straight up. That looks dramatic, and it is mostly what long silences always look like. With no closures, every name's participation fades at the same rate, so the whole field rises together. Across all sessions deep inside past silences (15 or more sessions in), the compass has a median of 0.91. This week's reading ranks at the 81st percentile of those. It is a strong version of the usual shape. The pace eased: the field's average drift fell from 0.150 to 0.124. The corner kept filling while the motion slowed, a deepening condition with an easing pace, not a reversal.

The six-month memory: the crowd lets go

The week's real change was in the six-month memory. There, most stocks had still been sitting in the lower-right crowd, in their normal range and tied to the market. That crowd lost 72 names in a week, from 270 to 198. They did not go to the breakaway corner, which held near 23. They went up. On net the middle strip gained 72 (44 to 116) and the strain corner gained 11 (7 to 18). The six-month compass reads 0.91, heading up and to the left, and its pace picked up this week. 84% of names moved left.

The strain corner deserves care, because Wednesday's read listed it as a catch-down marker. It went from 7 to 18 names, past the double digits Sunday's read named (Wednesday repeated it with a caveat). But look at who is there: Procter & Gamble, PepsiCo, CSX, Ecolab, FedEx, Ross, Aflac, Rockwell, DexCom, Eversource, Ingersoll Rand, Loews, NRG, Omnicom, Regency Centers, UDR, Align and A. O. Smith. It is a mix of mid-sized companies from nine sectors, mostly staples, industrials, insurers, utilities and property, with no large names among them. Together they are about 1.6% of the index. On this map the upper right means quiet and still tied, not under pressure. Apple, the largest name in Wednesday's strain list, has left it.

Jason put the six-month motion this way on Sunday morning: "It is still lifting, but lifting while sliding to the loose side… it is also getting monotonic with shear. It isn't 100%, but the vast majority… really vast… points to one motion or story." The instrument agrees. It can also connect each name's six-month position to its one-year position on the same day, a line the film calls the horizon shear. 86% of names sit further right, more tied, at six months than at a year. Their six-month motion is heading up and left, toward where the one-year memory already places them. The six-month picture is converging on the one-year picture. That is one geometry seen twice, and it counts once.

A construction event ahead · not market news

The six-month memory is a rolling window of 126 sessions. Today it reaches back to March 27. The April 9–15 release, this spring's burst of closures when hundreds of stocks crested together after the March correction, sits at its old edge. It drops out of the window over the next 9 to 13 sessions, around October 8–14. We expect that burst holds up much of the six-month crowd's tie to the market. When it leaves, the six-month picture will move on its own: the crowd, the strain count and the mean coupling. Any six-month reading in that stretch should carry this label.

Then and now · the spring silence and this one, through both memories

Two memories, traded places

The market's last long silence was this spring's correction, 30 sessions from February 25 to April 8. At its 18th session, March 20, the index was 5.6% below its last closure and the typical stock 6.8% below. The two memories then and now are close to mirror images, and the swap is still in place at session 22.

Wednesday's read cited a census of this shape (crowded at six months, loose at a year). What separated the mild outcomes from the severe ones was the one-year memory's coupling rising toward the crowd, as in autumn 2008. It has fallen again this week, to −0.06.

Chapter 5 · where each stock is in its own swing

Two groups on one dial

The short rhythm from Chapter 2 can be drawn as a clock. Each stock's price is compared with its own 20-session average, and its position in that swing becomes a position on a dial. Twelve o'clock is the top of the swing, which the instrument calls home. Six o'clock is the bottom, the trough. Stocks go around clockwise: over the top, down the right side, through the bottom and back up the left.

The clock has two hands. The count hand averages every stock equally. The weight hand weights each stock by market value, the way the index does. A hand's length says how much the stocks agree, from 0 to 1. A hand shorter than about a third is a zero: the stocks are spread around the dial and its direction means nothing.

On screen the clock plays the five weeks from August 24 and can show the 70-stock room alone; the page shows Friday for all 503. A hand shorter than the dashed ring (0.35) is a zero.

On Friday, 63% of stocks sat just past the bottom of their swing, turning up, and 22% sat just past the top. The count's hand points to about 7:45 on the dial with a length of 0.39, barely coherent. Over the week it moved from 0.54 to 0.65 of a cycle. The crowd is climbing slowly and has not reached home.

By market value the picture splits. 53% of the index's value sits just past home and 36% sits just past the trough, on opposite sides of the dial. The weight's hand is a zero (0.18), and it stayed a zero all week, never longer than 0.29. It has been a zero for twelve sessions in a row. Nvidia, Meta, Tesla and Micron crested on Monday or Tuesday, and Apple a few days earlier. On Friday those five, with Microsoft and Alphabet, all sat between 0.10 and 0.19 of a cycle, a little past the top. (Alphabet's newest readings have swung across home twice this week; treat its exact position as a sketch.) Amazon (0.61) and Broadcom (0.68) are climbing with the crowd.

Sol, who reviews these reads with us, summed the week up as "one vector, two clocks." The two clocks are real, with one correction. The split is not only in the weight. The count has a second measure, R2, that is high when stocks gather at two opposite points instead of one. On Friday it read 0.60, the 97th percentile of the record. The count itself is two groups: the leaders' rooms, whose smaller members crested with them, and everyone else. The weight's version reads 0.70. By sector, 97% of utilities, 93% of property companies and 83% of financials sit just past the trough. Technology has 49% of its names just past home.

In the record, a coherent count with a weight hand under 0.25 has been ordinary: 120 episodes, a next-month median of +1.4% (62% up) and a 10th percentile of −4.2%, against +1.3%, 66% and −4.7% for any session. The split tells us where the market's parts are. It has not told us which way the index goes next.

How soft is the edge? The phase is computed with a transform that uses the whole price series, so its newest few readings move when new sessions arrive. This week showed how far. Wednesday's read printed Monday's count at 0.63 of a cycle, strength 0.48. Today Monday reads 0.54, strength 0.41. It printed 47% of the index's value just past home on Monday. Today Monday reads 22%. The megacaps sat right on the home boundary, and a shift of a few hundredths of a cycle moved a quarter of the index's value across it. Read the hands and the week's direction. Treat the newest day's value-by-quarter as a sketch; this week it moved by 25 points.

Reading the dial. Check each hand's strength first: below 0.35 its direction is not a position. The count hand, the weight hand, names by quarter and value by quarter are four separate statements; one crowded quarter does not rescue a zero hand. Use the raster to ask whether today's split assembled, held or is coming apart. A single stock's newest phase is the softest number on any of these screens.

Chapter 6 · the two books: amplitude and phase

The anchors let go

The phase clock asks where each stock is in its swing. The amplitude book asks whether the size of the stocks' swings looks alike across the market, measured against each stock's own history. It asks at sixteen memory lengths, called rungs, from one month (21 sessions) up to three years (756). When the swings are unusually alike, the market is moving as one body. When they are unusually scattered, every stock is doing its own thing.

The book has two kinds of agreement event, and Jason calls them the anchors. A locked zero is a day when the one-year rung's spread falls below the bottom tenth of its own past year. Wednesday's read called the locked zeros around the Fed "the note". An anchored zero applies the same test at whichever rung agrees most that day. The board draws them in a lane: each anchored zero sits at its rung, gold when the one-year rung is locked too, blue when only the anchored rung agrees.

This rewrites one line of Wednesday's read. It said the note appeared to have broken on Friday, September 18, by a hair (1.158 against a floor of 1.122). Several builds later Friday reads 1.113 against 1.121, a locked zero after all. The locked run now covers the five sessions from September 14 to 18, and the break came on Monday. From there the spread opened fast. Monday reads 1.152, just above the floor. Tuesday reads 1.229, Wednesday 1.375 and Thursday 1.341. Wednesday's value is above 91% of all days since 2000. Friday printed 1.548. Every first print so far has settled lower.

The memory spectrogram shows the same week across all sixteen rungs. Each cell is one rung on one day. Rust means the stocks' swing sizes are unusually alike at that memory. White is ordinary. Blue means unusually scattered. Deep memories sit at the top.

"We've got anchors firing, S1 126 firing, and somehow the right edge of the spectrogram has gone blue in the SMOOTHED display. That is the tendency of the raw edge, not smoothed… interesting."

Jason Connerty, Sunday morning, from the board

That answers Jason's question. The smoothed panel normally hides a one-day flash at the edge. It turned blue because the blue held from Wednesday to Friday, and Wednesday and Thursday have already settled once or twice without losing it. Wednesday's read made two predictions about this chart. It said Monday's all-blue column would fade, and it did: Monday now reads 0.22 to 0.83 across the rungs. It also said the deep rust was the more durable part of the picture. That one was wrong. The rust was gone by Monday, and by Wednesday the blue had climbed to the 441-session rung, with the deepest rungs pale behind it.

The board's ruler, which counts rungs pinned at either end of their own history, has printed the scatter end every day this week: half the rungs on Monday, all sixteen on Wednesday and Thursday, eleven on Friday. On Friday's print, 5.9% of names were unusually loud against their own history and 2.5% unusually quiet. That is Jason's reading of the ruler: "Loud tail is getting loud at last reading, but there is still a quiet section… not much though."

For context, three sessions in a row with 11 or more of 16 raw rungs blue has happened in 45 separate episodes since 2002. Over the next month the index's median was +0.8% (56% up), with a 10th percentile of −7.5% and a worst dip within the month of −9.7% at the 10th percentile. That is a fatter left tail than an ordinary session (−4.7% and −6.8%). But 91% of those episodes came within two sessions of a closure, which is when blue usually appears. Only two came inside a long silence: June 2002 (−13.6% over the next month) and January 2005 (+3.1%). Two cases don't make a lean, and this week's version is still settling.

The phase book: the contender has a history

The second book asks a different question: at what memory length is the market's burst energy most tightly tied to its drawdowns? The Waves view tracks the answer day by day. The incumbent is a 372-session structure, positively coupled at +0.889. Its family (360 sessions at first, 372 since September 10) has held control for 16 sessions, since September 3. The strongest alternative on Friday was a 180-session structure, anti-coupled at −0.807, 0.08 short of the incumbent. Its handoff distance is 3, the ceiling that means it has no presence in the settled book. By the rule it is not a challenger.

It has a history, though. An anti-coupled structure from the same family, at 156 and then 168 sessions, was the day's top structure from August 14 to September 2: the fourteen sessions right after the index's record, including the start of the silence. In the settled book it held control from about August 18 to September 4. It faded in early September and the coupled family took over: 360 sessions from September 3, then 372 from September 10. This week the family came back. It showed at 252 sessions on Monday to Wednesday (−0.68 to −0.73), then at 180 as the leading alternative on Thursday (−0.82) and Friday (−0.81). Jason put it simply: "The waves view shows that contender… not challenging, but not going away." The sign says nothing about price direction; it describes how burst energy and drawdown depth have been paired at that memory.

The whole-market rails

The floor-loss signature (S1) has been lit at the six-month horizon since August 20: 26 sessions. Of 34 past runs, the median lasted 12, and five lasted this long (April 2017, August 2017, February 2020, October 2021, January 2025). Three of those five lit a second horizon, the escalation Wednesday's read listed as a roll-through marker, but all three did it within their first three weeks. The two that were still on one horizon at 26 sessions never escalated. This one is still on one. The story count, the number of independent directions the stocks' returns are moving in, rose from 0.92 of its norm in Wednesday's build (Monday's close) to 0.97 (15 effective stories). The storms of the past began below 0.55. The market is telling more stories, not fewer.

Chapter 7 · what the week restated, and the fork graded

Graded, not resolved

A weekly read has two jobs at the end. First it separates what the instrument said at the time from what it says now, because the newest days of several of these measures are revised as sessions arrive. Then it grades the fork against the markers named before the outcome.

Catch-up lost ground: the typical stock fell again and the gap widened. Catch-down gained a little: the leaders crested and strain grew. But the marker that most clearly separated mild outcomes from severe ones in the record, the one-year memory's coupling, moved the mild way. Neither road's decisive marker fired. The weekly-read rule allows for this. A completed week does not need a completed market outcome, and a fork that has live evidence on both branches stays open.

Read across the rows and the record says three things. First, the fat-tailed shape Wednesday's read worried about has passed. Second, the rows with fatter tails today are the blue spectrogram, which is still settling and usually shows up right after a closure rather than deep in a silence, and, mildly, the long silence itself. Third, as on Wednesday, the most important fact is the row with no history. Every earlier release started from a fallen index.

The film's nearest-shape finder lists January 2008, October 2018, March 2023, September 2025 and June 2024 as the five past stretches most like the last twenty sessions. The largest drops within the following three months were 8%, 16%, 0%, 2% and 5%. Its honesty score is 0.52, meaning it sorts later slides from non-slides about as well as a coin, so it is printed because it is on the screen, not because it tells us anything.

Three reads

This read went in rounds. Jason asked Sol, the project's second reader (ChatGPT), for a read of the week, then gave his own from the live views, and the two talked it through. Claude read last, from the data, with both in hand.

"Yeah… I agree with you overall… it feels… unsettled. But not yet broken."

Jason Connerty, Sunday morning, from the live views

"One vector, two clocks. The market is not broken. But the internals are increasingly moving as though they recognize the same deterioration."

Sol, Sunday morning, after Jason's read

My read

This section is interpretation, not the instrument. The index held its level this week because its heaviest names held. Seventy stocks that had spent six weeks assembling into a single AI-hardware trade, whose core crested on Tuesday, gained 3% weighted by value and supplied half of the gain. Meta, Microsoft and AMD supplied the other half. The median of the other 433 stocks lost about 1%. Underneath, every part of the instrument moved further apart. The field kept floating and loosening. The six-month crowd, the last place the market still looked like one body, let go of 72 names. The amplitude book's anchors let go, and by Wednesday no memory agreed. The anti-coupled contender came back in the phase book.

What did not happen matters as much. No closure fired, red or green. The one-year memory did not couple; it loosened. The floor-loss signature stayed on one horizon. The story count rose. The weight's hand never firmed on the falling side. That is what Jason means by unsettled but not broken, and I agree. On Sol's shift toward catch-down, I would hold the lean at even. The catch-down mechanism is visible in the room. Its core is half a cycle ahead of the rest of the market and moving at the same speed, so if the next closure comes from the crowd reaching home and both keep that pace, the core will be well into its descent by then, and that closure would tend to fire on a soft index. But the mechanism has been visible since Friday's notebook, and so far the leaders are drifting past their crest, not falling. Sol's "one vector" is mostly the ordinary lift of a long silence. The part that isn't ordinary is the six-month crowd letting go, on a lens that loses its April anchor in two weeks.

Toward catch-down, I would want to see the room's weight hand cross 0.25 while the room holds together, a closure on a red day, or the one-year coupling turning up. Toward catch-up, I would want the crowd's hand past 0.8 with the market's weight hand firming on the same side, or a broad green release. Until one of those, the gap is the story, and the room and a few megacaps are what is holding it open.

What is observed, what is interpretation, what is not established

Observed

  • S&P +1.2% on the week, all of it Monday. Median stock −0.70%, equal-weight −0.25%, 43% of stocks up.
  • Since Aug 13: index −0.7%, median stock −6.1%. Gap −5.4 points, the widest in 818 near-high sessions; every session this week beyond the old extreme.
  • 22 sessions since a closure. All 19 past silences this long had the index lower. Here +0.9%, with the median stock −5.4%.
  • The 70-stock room: median +1.7%, 0.63 of the week's 1.26 value-weighted points; Meta, Microsoft and AMD 0.76; the other 430 stocks −0.13. 65 of 70 together after the freeze.
  • One year: 96% quiet, 20 below the floor, 209 in the breakaway, 81 in and 0 out. Six months: crowd 270 → 198, strain 7 → 18.
  • Count 0.39 at 0.65; the weight a zero for 12 sessions; the count's R2 at the 97th percentile.
  • Locked zeros Sep 10 and 14–18, anchored zeros Sep 9–21, then no agreeing rung. Wednesday settled at the 91st percentile so far.
  • Phase book: 372 at +0.889, streak 16; alternative 180 at −0.807, distance 3. S1 at six months for 26 sessions. Story count 0.97.

Interpretation

  • The gap held because the heaviest names held: one room, plus Meta, Microsoft and AMD.
  • The silence, the breadth gap and the room are one fact seen three ways.
  • The six-month crowd letting go and the horizon shear are one geometry.
  • The compass's high reading is the silence's ordinary lift. The leftward drift is the informative part.
  • Catch-down's mechanism is visible in the room's timing but has not acted. The lean is even.

Not established

  • Which way the gap closes. There is no precedent for this starting point.
  • That the room causes anything outside itself.
  • That the anti-coupled branch says anything about price direction.
  • How the six-month memory will look once the April release leaves its window.
  • Calibrated probabilities. The census conditions were written after looking, on one roster with survivorship.

The words, in plain terms

Closure
A day on which at least 8% of the stocks the instrument tracks (59 today) reach the top of their own short swing together. The market's ordinary heartbeat.
Silence · release
A run of sessions with no closure, usually a slide. The release is the closure that ends it.
The floor · the float
On the map, each stock's own normal level of participation in the market's shared moves. In a silence every stock's participation fades on the same 21-session half-life and the field drifts up off the floor together: the float.
Breakaway · crowd · strain · middle strip
Regions of the map. Breakaway: out of range and on its own (upper left). Crowd: in range and tied (lower right). Strain: out of range yet tied (upper right). The middle strip lies between, out of range and partly tied.
Turnstile · compass
Names entering vs leaving the breakaway over five sessions. How uniformly the whole field moved over five sessions (0 to 1) and which way.
Memory (lens) · horizon shear
How much history a measurement uses: one year (252 sessions) or six months (126). The shear links each stock's position through the two memories on the same day.
Room
A group of stocks that have been moving with each other rather than with the market, rebuilt each day by Burst Currents. A frozen set keeps the names fixed so they can be followed.
Home · trough · the two hands
The top and bottom of a stock's own short swing. The count's hand averages every stock once; the weight's hand weights them by market value. Length 0–1 is agreement. Under 0.35 is a zero.
R2
A second measure of the same stocks that is high when they gather at two opposite points. A low hand with a high R2 means two groups, not a scatter.
Rung · the spectrogram
One memory length, from 21 to 756 sessions. The spectrogram shows every rung's spread each day: rust alike, white ordinary, blue scattered.
Locked zero · anchored zero · the anchors
A locked zero: the one-year rung's spread falls below the bottom tenth of its past year ("the note"). An anchored zero: the same test at whichever rung agrees most that day. Jason calls them the anchors.
Phase book · incumbent · handoff distance
The memory length at which burst energy and drawdowns are most tightly tied. The incumbent controls the settled book. Handoff distance counts the prints a challenger needs; 3 is the ceiling, meaning no challenge.
S1 floor loss · story count
A structural signature lit at one or more horizons. The story count is how many independent directions the stocks' returns move in, against its own norm.
The edge
The newest few readings of anything built on the whole-history transform. They restate as sessions arrive, so treat them as sketches.
